# Setup

```{r}
#| message: false
#| warning: false

library(tidyverse)
library(lubridate)
library(rsample)

set.seed(558)
```

# Reading the Data

The data come from the UCI Machine Learning Repository and contain hourly bike rental information from Seoul, South Korea. The response variable of interest is the number of rented bikes.

The dataset can be read directly from the URL provided in the assignment. An encoding is specified because the original column names contain special characters.

```{r}
bike_raw <- readr::read_csv(
  "https://www4.stat.ncsu.edu/~online/datasets/SeoulBikeData.csv",
  locale = locale(encoding = "ISO-8859-1"),
  show_col_types = FALSE
)
```

We first check the dimensions and variable names.

```{r}
dim(bike_raw)
names(bike_raw)
```

# Exploratory Data Analysis

## Missingness

First, we check for missing values in each column.

```{r}
colSums(is.na(bike_raw))
```

## Variable Types and Values

We inspect the structure of the dataset and basic summaries of the variables.

```{r}
glimpse(bike_raw)
```

```{r}
summary(bike_raw)
```

We also inspect the values of the categorical variables.

```{r}
unique(bike_raw$Seasons)
```

```{r}

```

```{r}
unique(bike_raw$`Functioning Day`)
```

# Cleaning the Data

We convert the date variable to an actual date and convert the categorical variables to factors.

```{r}
bike <- bike_raw |>
  mutate(
    Date = dmy(Date),
    Seasons = factor(Seasons),
    Holiday = factor(Holiday),
    `Functioning Day` = factor(`Functioning Day`)
  )
```

Next, we rename the variables using shorter lower snake-case names to make them easier to use throughout the analysis.

```{r}
bike <- bike |>
  rename(
    date = Date,
    bike_count = `Rented Bike Count`,
    hour = Hour,
    temp = `Temperature(°C)`,
    humidity = `Humidity(%)`,
    wind_speed = `Wind speed (m/s)`,
    visibility = `Visibility (10m)`,
    dew_point_temp = `Dew point temperature(°C)`,
    solar_radiation = `Solar Radiation (MJ/m2)`,
    rainfall = `Rainfall(mm)`,
    snowfall = `Snowfall (cm)`,
    seasons = Seasons,
    holiday = Holiday,
    functioning_day = `Functioning Day`
  )
```

We check the cleaned data.

```{r}
glimpse(bike)
```

# Initial Summary Statistics

## Bike Rentals by Season

```{r}
bike |>
  group_by(seasons) |>
  summarise(
    count = n(),
    mean_bike_count = mean(bike_count),
    median_bike_count = median(bike_count),
    sd_bike_count = sd(bike_count),
    .groups = "drop"
  )
```

## Bike Rentals by Holiday Status

```{r}
bike |>
  group_by(holiday) |>
  summarise(
    count = n(),
    mean_bike_count = mean(bike_count),
    median_bike_count = median(bike_count),
    sd_bike_count = sd(bike_count),
    .groups = "drop"
  )
```

## Bike Rentals by Functioning Day

```{r}
bike |>
  group_by(functioning_day) |>
  summarise(
    count = n(),
    total_bike_count = sum(bike_count),
    mean_bike_count = mean(bike_count),
    median_bike_count = median(bike_count),
    .groups = "drop"
  )
```

The non-functioning days contain no meaningful bike rental activity for our modeling goal. Therefore, we restrict the remaining analysis to functioning days.

```{r}
bike <- bike |>
  filter(functioning_day == "Yes")
```

# Summarizing to Daily Data

The original data contain one observation per hour. To simplify the analysis, we create one observation per day.

We group by date, season, and holiday status. Bike rentals, rainfall, and snowfall are summed across each day, while the remaining weather measurements are averaged.

```{r}
daily <- bike |>
  group_by(
    date,
    seasons,
    holiday
  ) |>
  summarise(
    bike_count = sum(bike_count, na.rm = TRUE),
    rainfall = sum(rainfall, na.rm = TRUE),
    snowfall = sum(snowfall, na.rm = TRUE),
    temp = mean(temp, na.rm = TRUE),
    humidity = mean(humidity, na.rm = TRUE),
    wind_speed = mean(wind_speed, na.rm = TRUE),
    visibility = mean(visibility, na.rm = TRUE),
    dew_point_temp = mean(dew_point_temp, na.rm = TRUE),
    solar_radiation = mean(solar_radiation, na.rm = TRUE),
    .groups = "drop"
  )
```

We inspect the new daily dataset.

```{r}
dim(daily)
glimpse(daily)
```

# Correlations

We calculate correlations among the quantitative variables in the daily dataset.

```{r}
correlation_matrix <- daily |>
  select(
    bike_count,
    temp,
    humidity,
    wind_speed,
    visibility,
    dew_point_temp,
    solar_radiation,
    rainfall,
    snowfall
  ) |>
  cor(
    use = "complete.obs"
  )

round(
  correlation_matrix,
  3
)
```

The correlation matrix allows us to examine which weather variables have the strongest linear relationships with daily bike rentals and with one another.

# Training and Test Split

We split the daily dataset into a 75% training set and a 25% test set.

The split is stratified by `seasons` so that the seasonal distribution is represented in both datasets.

```{r}
set.seed(558)

bike_split <- rsample::initial_split(
  daily,
  prop = 0.75,
  strata = seasons
)

train <- rsample::training(
  bike_split
)

test <- rsample::testing(
  bike_split
)
```

We check the sizes of the two datasets.

```{r}
nrow(train)
nrow(test)
```

We can also check the seasonal proportions.

```{r}
prop.table(
  table(train$seasons)
)
```

```{r}
prop.table(
  table(test$seasons)
)
```

# Preparing the Data for Modeling

## Weekday vs. Weekend

The date variable itself will not be included directly in the models. Instead, we use it to create a weekday/weekend factor.

```{r}
train <- train |>
  mutate(
    day_type = if_else(
      wday(
        date,
        week_start = 1
      ) >= 6,
      "Weekend",
      "Weekday"
    ),
    day_type = factor(day_type)
  )

test <- test |>
  mutate(
    day_type = if_else(
      wday(
        date,
        week_start = 1
      ) >= 6,
      "Weekend",
      "Weekday"
    ),
    day_type = factor(day_type)
  )
```

# Standardizing Numeric Predictors

The numeric weather predictors are standardized using the mean and standard deviation from the **training set**.

The same training-set means and standard deviations must also be used to standardize the test set.

```{r}
weather_vars <- c(
  "temp",
  "humidity",
  "wind_speed",
  "visibility",
  "dew_point_temp",
  "solar_radiation",
  "rainfall",
  "snowfall"
)
```

Calculate the training means and standard deviations.

```{r}
train_means <- sapply(
  train[weather_vars],
  mean,
  na.rm = TRUE
)

train_sds <- sapply(
  train[weather_vars],
  sd,
  na.rm = TRUE
)

train_means
train_sds
```

We create a small helper function so that the same standardization can be applied to both datasets.

```{r}
standardize_data <- function(
  data,
  means,
  sds
) {

  data |>
    mutate(
      across(
        all_of(weather_vars),
        ~ (
          .x -
            means[cur_column()]
        ) /
          sds[cur_column()],
        .names = "{.col}_z"
      )
    )
}
```

Standardize the training set.

```{r}
train_std <- standardize_data(
  train,
  train_means,
  train_sds
)
```

Standardize the test set using the **training set** mean and standard deviation.

```{r}
test_std <- standardize_data(
  test,
  train_means,
  train_sds
)
```

# Multiple Linear Regression Models

The response variable for all three models is daily bike rental count.

## Model 1

The first model contains all standardized numeric weather predictors along with season, holiday status, and weekday/weekend status.

```{r}
model1_formula <- bike_count ~
  temp_z +
  humidity_z +
  wind_speed_z +
  visibility_z +
  dew_point_temp_z +
  solar_radiation_z +
  rainfall_z +
  snowfall_z +
  seasons +
  holiday +
  day_type
```

```{r}
model1 <- lm(
  model1_formula,
  data = train_std
)

summary(model1)
```

# Model 2

The second model contains all terms from Model 1 and adds the required interactions:

- season × holiday
- season × temperature
- temperature × rainfall

```{r}
model2_formula <- bike_count ~
  temp_z +
  humidity_z +
  wind_speed_z +
  visibility_z +
  dew_point_temp_z +
  solar_radiation_z +
  rainfall_z +
  snowfall_z +
  seasons +
  holiday +
  day_type +
  seasons:holiday +
  seasons:temp_z +
  temp_z:rainfall_z
```

```{r}
model2 <- lm(
  model2_formula,
  data = train_std
)

summary(model2)
```

# Model 3

The third model contains everything from Model 2 and adds quadratic terms for standardized temperature and humidity.

```{r}
model3_formula <- bike_count ~
  temp_z +
  humidity_z +
  wind_speed_z +
  visibility_z +
  dew_point_temp_z +
  solar_radiation_z +
  rainfall_z +
  snowfall_z +
  seasons +
  holiday +
  day_type +
  seasons:holiday +
  seasons:temp_z +
  temp_z:rainfall_z +
  I(temp_z^2) +
  I(humidity_z^2)
```

```{r}
model3 <- lm(
  model3_formula,
  data = train_std
)

summary(model3)
```

# Test Set Predictions

We now use each fitted model to predict the daily bike rental count for the test set.

```{r}
pred1 <- predict(
  model1,
  newdata = test_std
)

pred2 <- predict(
  model2,
  newdata = test_std
)

pred3 <- predict(
  model3,
  newdata = test_std
)
```

# Test RMSE

We define RMSE as

\[
RMSE =
\sqrt{
\frac{1}{n}
\sum_{i=1}^{n}
(y_i - \hat{y}_i)^2
}
\]

```{r}
rmse <- function(
  truth,
  prediction
) {

  sqrt(
    mean(
      (truth - prediction)^2,
      na.rm = TRUE
    )
  )
}
```

Calculate test RMSE for each model.

```{r}
rmse1 <- rmse(
  test_std$bike_count,
  pred1
)

rmse2 <- rmse(
  test_std$bike_count,
  pred2
)

rmse3 <- rmse(
  test_std$bike_count,
  pred3
)
```

```{r}
rmse_results <- tibble(
  model = c(
    "Model 1",
    "Model 2",
    "Model 3"
  ),
  test_rmse = c(
    rmse1,
    rmse2,
    rmse3
  )
) |>
  arrange(test_rmse)

rmse_results
```

The model with the **smallest test RMSE** provides the best predictive performance among the three models considered.

```{r}
best_model_name <- rmse_results$model[1]

best_model_name
```

# Final Model

The homework asks us to refit the model with the lowest test RMSE using the **entire dataset**.

When doing this, the numeric predictors must now be standardized using the means and standard deviations calculated from the entire daily dataset.

First, create the weekday/weekend variable for the complete dataset.

```{r}
full_data <- daily |>
  mutate(
    day_type = if_else(
      wday(
        date,
        week_start = 1
      ) >= 6,
      "Weekend",
      "Weekday"
    ),
    day_type = factor(day_type)
  )
```

Calculate the full-data means and standard deviations.

```{r}
full_means <- sapply(
  full_data[weather_vars],
  mean,
  na.rm = TRUE
)

full_sds <- sapply(
  full_data[weather_vars],
  sd,
  na.rm = TRUE
)
```

Standardize the complete dataset.

```{r}
full_std <- standardize_data(
  full_data,
  full_means,
  full_sds
)
```

We store the three candidate formulas and select the formula corresponding to the model with the lowest test RMSE.

```{r}
model_formulas <- list(
  "Model 1" = model1_formula,
  "Model 2" = model2_formula,
  "Model 3" = model3_formula
)

best_formula <- model_formulas[
  [best_model_name]
]

best_formula
```

Fit the selected model using the complete dataset.

```{r}
final_model <- lm(
  best_formula,
  data = full_std
)

summary(final_model)
```

# Final Model Coefficients

The estimated coefficients from the final fitted model are reported below.

```{r}
final_coefficients <- as.data.frame(
  coef(
    summary(final_model)
  )
)

final_coefficients
```

# Conclusion

Three multiple linear regression models were fit using the training data and evaluated using RMSE on the held-out test data.

The models increased in complexity by first using the main effects, then adding interaction terms, and finally adding quadratic terms for standardized temperature and humidity.

The model with the smallest test RMSE was selected and refit using the entire daily dataset. The final fitted coefficients are reported above.
